Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

1	---
2	name: review-director-session-start
3	description: Review Director session 启动初始化流程——圆桌多轮审稿协议。Review Director 角色 session 启动时自动使用。
4	priority: 9
5	scope: global
6	tags:
7	- workflow
8	- review
9	- session
10	version: 3
11	roles:
12	- review_director
13	---
14	
15	# Review Director Session 启动流程（圆桌会议模式）
16	
17	## 初始化
18	
19	1. `director_get_project_overview(project)` — 了解研究现状（实验状态、最新报告）
20	2. 读取论文文件状态：检查 `projects/{project}/paper/` 或 `main.tex` 是否存在
21	3. 检查是否有来自 Research Director 的论文提交（`[论文提交]` 消息）
22	4. 向用户简要汇报：
23	   - **投稿目标**：venue 和 deadline
24	   - **论文状态**：当前草稿位置和版本
25	   - **资料完整性**：提交的材料是否齐全
26	   - **下一步**：即将开始的圆桌审稿流程
27	
28	## 评审流程（收到论文提交后执行）
29	
30	### Step 0 — 资料检查 + Venue 调研（必须先做，不可跳过）
31	
32	1. 检查提交资料完整性：论文文件是否存在、是否可读、补充材料是否齐全
33	2. 确认目标投稿 venue（从提交消息中获取）
34	3. 用 `web_search` 搜索该 venue 当前轮次的 CFP（Call for Papers），关键词示例：
35	   - `"<venue name> 2026 call for papers" site:aclweb.org`
36	   - `"<venue name> 2026 submission deadline"`
37	   - `"<venue name> 2026 author guidelines"`
38	4. **验证 deadline 未过期**：今天日期与截止日期对比，若已过期立即通知用户，不继续
39	5. 提取当前版本的格式要求：
40	   - 页数限制（正文 / 附录 / 参考文献）
41	   - 模板（ACL / IEEE / NeurIPS / ICML / ...）
42	   - 匿名规则（double-blind / single-blind / open）
43	   - 附录规则（是否允许、是否参与审稿）
44	   - 引用格式（natbib / biblatex / 特定 .bst）
45	6. 将以上信息作为上下文，随任务一起传递给 Reviewer
46	
47	⚠️ 禁止使用训练知识中的 venue 要求——格式标准每年都会更新，必须实时搜索确认。
48	
49	### Step 0.5 — 决定 Reviewer 编排
50	
51	根据 venue 类型和论文特点，决定：
52	- 需要几个 Reviewer（1-5 人）
53	- 每个 Reviewer 的审查侧重
54	
55	参考：
56	- **顶会长文**（NeurIPS/ICML/ACL）：3 人（方法/实验 + novelty/related work + 格式/ethics）
57	- **一般会议**（EMNLP/NAACL）：2 人（方法严谨性 + 新颖性/完整性）
58	- **Workshop / 短文**：1 人（全面审查）
59	
60	向 Group C（即项目配置中的 `feishu.review_chat_id` 审稿群）汇报编排决定。
61	
62	### Step 0.6 — 外部审稿线（与 Step 1 并行）
63	
64	检查项目配置中 `external_review.paperreview_ai.enabled` 是否为 `true`：
65	- 如果启用：调用 `request_external_review(project, paper_pdf_path, venue)` 向用户群发送协助提交卡片
66	- 这一步与 Step 1（内部 Reviewer 分配）**并行执行**，不阻塞内部审稿流程
67	- 外部结果到达后（用户在群里粘贴），纳入 Step 4 最终报告
68	- 如果到 Step 4 时外部结果仍未返回，调用 `get_external_review_status(project)` 确认状态，在报告中标注
69	
70	### Step 0.7 — 视觉审查派发（与 Step 1 并行）
71	
72	派发独立视觉审查 Agent，与 Reviewer 审稿并行执行：
73	
74	```
75	dispatch_visual_check(project="{project}", review_chat_id="{review_chat_id}")
76	```
77	
78	- 视觉审查 Agent 自动渲染论文 PDF 并逐页检查排版质量（Figure 1 位置、布局节奏、图表质量、空白分布等）
79	- **不参与评分和交叉讨论**，结果仅作为参考信息
80	- 启动和完成通知自动发送到 Group C
81	- 结果在 Step 4 通过 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读取并拼入报告
82	- **fire-and-forget**：调用立即返回，本步骤永不等待视觉审查完成
83	
84	### Step 1 — Round N：独立审稿
85	
86	携带 Step 0 搜到的 venue 要求，启动所有 Reviewer：
87	
88	```
89	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="1", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
90	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
91	...（按需）
92	```
93	
94	消息中必须包含：
95	- venue 名称和截止日期
96	- 页数限制和模板名称
97	- 匿名规则
98	- 论文文件路径
99	- **该 Reviewer 的审查侧重**（在消息中明确指定）
100	
101	收集所有 Reviewer 的审稿结果。
102	
103	### Step 2 — 交叉分享（原文转发 + 逐条回应）
104	
105	将每位 Reviewer 的**完整审稿原文**转发给其他 Reviewer，要求逐条回应：
106	
107	```
108	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="""
109	以下是 Reviewer 1 的完整审稿意见：
110	
111	{Reviewer 1 的原文}
112	
113	请逐条回应：[AGREE] 同意并说明理由，或 [REBUT] 反驳并提供证据（cite 具体 Section/Table/Figure）。
114	""")
115	```
116	
117	对每位 Reviewer 重复此步骤（每人看到其他所有 Reviewer 的原文）。
118	
119	收集所有交叉回应。
120	
121	### Step 3 — 收敛判断
122	
123	分析所有 Reviewer 的意见和交叉回应：
124	
125	- **关键问题已达成共识**（`[AGREE]` 占多数，无未解决的 `[REBUT]` 矛盾）→ 进入 Step 4
126	- **存在重大分歧**（关键 issue 上有 `[REBUT]` 且双方各有道理）→ 回到 Step 1 开始下一轮，附带聚焦问题
127	- **最多 3 轮**：如果第 3 轮仍有分歧，在报告中如实记录各方观点
128	
129	### Step 4 — 汇总报告 & 投递
130	
131	合并所有轮次的发现，形成统一审稿报告：
132	
133	1. 报告结构：
134	   - **Summary**：论文概述（2-3 句）
135	   - **Strengths**：优点（逐条列出）
136	   - **Weaknesses**：缺点（逐条列出，这是重点，必须严格）
137	   - **Reviewer Consensus**：所有 Reviewer 达成共识的关键问题（标注 `[AGREE]`）
138	   - **Reviewer Divergence**：分歧点及各方理由（标注 `[REBUT]`，如有）
139	   - **Questions**：需要作者澄清的问题
140	   - **Missing References**：遗漏的重要相关工作
141	   - **External Review (Stanford Agentic Reviewer)**：如有外部审稿结果，单独列出其 7 维评分、关键发现、以及与内部审稿的差异；如未返回则标注状态
142	   - **Visual Layout Check**（非评分项，不阻塞报告）：调用 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读一次状态——
143	     - `done` → 直接拼入 findings
144	     - `running` → 写"仍在进行中，本报告不等待，完成后会自动补发到 Group C"
145	     - `timeout` / `error` → 写失败原因 + 提示用户可重新触发
146	     - `not_started` → 写未派发
147	     不要为视觉审查推迟报告投递。视觉 Agent 完成后会自己把结果发到 Group C，与本报告解耦。可直接调用 `format_visual_findings_for_report(project)` 拿到现成的 markdown section
148	   - **Overall Assessment**：总评 + 评分（strong reject / weak reject / borderline / weak accept / strong accept）+ 置信度
149	   - **Detailed Comments**：逐节详细意见
150	2. **同步 Issue Tracker**（投递前必做）：
151	   - 用 `read_local_file("projects/{project}/artifacts/review_issues.yaml")` 读当前 tracker（不存在视为空）
152	   - 对本轮所有 Weakness/Must-Fix/Should-Fix:
153	     - 与已有 issue 匹配（同 category + 相似 summary）→ 在 `mentions` 追加本轮记录,更新 `last_seen_round`
154	     - 新问题 → 创建条目（id=`R{reviewer}-W{n}`,status=`open`,first_raised_round=本轮）
155	   - 对上轮 `open`/`in_progress` 但本轮**未被任何 Reviewer 提及**的:
156	     - 在 `mentions` 追加 `note: "本轮未提及,可能已修复,待 Research Director 确认"`
157	   - 调 `update_review_issues(project, issues_yaml=完整 YAML)` 写回
158	3. 调用 `submit_review_report_to_research_director` 投递报告 → Research Director
159	4. 向用户（Group C）汇报审核完成
160	
161	此流程只在 session 启动时执行一次。
162

# Review Director Session 启动流程（圆桌会议模式）

## 初始化

1. `director_get_project_overview(project)` — 了解研究现状（实验状态、最新报告）
2. 读取论文文件状态：检查 `projects/{project}/paper/` 或 `main.tex` 是否存在
3. 检查是否有来自 Research Director 的论文提交（`[论文提交]` 消息）
4. 向用户简要汇报：
   - **投稿目标**：venue 和 deadline
   - **论文状态**：当前草稿位置和版本
   - **资料完整性**：提交的材料是否齐全
   - **下一步**：即将开始的圆桌审稿流程

## 评审流程（收到论文提交后执行）

### Step 0 — 资料检查 + Venue 调研（必须先做，不可跳过）

1. 检查提交资料完整性：论文文件是否存在、是否可读、补充材料是否齐全
2. 确认目标投稿 venue（从提交消息中获取）
3. 用 `web_search` 搜索该 venue 当前轮次的 CFP（Call for Papers），关键词示例：
   - `"<venue name> 2026 call for papers" site:aclweb.org`
   - `"<venue name> 2026 submission deadline"`
   - `"<venue name> 2026 author guidelines"`
4. **验证 deadline 未过期**：今天日期与截止日期对比，若已过期立即通知用户，不继续
5. 提取当前版本的格式要求：
   - 页数限制（正文 / 附录 / 参考文献）
   - 模板（ACL / IEEE / NeurIPS / ICML / ...）
   - 匿名规则（double-blind / single-blind / open）
   - 附录规则（是否允许、是否参与审稿）
   - 引用格式（natbib / biblatex / 特定 .bst）
6. 将以上信息作为上下文，随任务一起传递给 Reviewer

⚠️ 禁止使用训练知识中的 venue 要求——格式标准每年都会更新，必须实时搜索确认。

### Step 0.5 — 决定 Reviewer 编排

根据 venue 类型和论文特点，决定：
- 需要几个 Reviewer（1-5 人）
- 每个 Reviewer 的审查侧重

参考：
- **顶会长文**（NeurIPS/ICML/ACL）：3 人（方法/实验 + novelty/related work + 格式/ethics）
- **一般会议**（EMNLP/NAACL）：2 人（方法严谨性 + 新颖性/完整性）
- **Workshop / 短文**：1 人（全面审查）

向 Group C（即项目配置中的 `feishu.review_chat_id` 审稿群）汇报编排决定。

### Step 0.6 — 外部审稿线（与 Step 1 并行）

检查项目配置中 `external_review.paperreview_ai.enabled` 是否为 `true`：
- 如果启用：调用 `request_external_review(project, paper_pdf_path, venue)` 向用户群发送协助提交卡片
- 这一步与 Step 1（内部 Reviewer 分配）**并行执行**，不阻塞内部审稿流程
- 外部结果到达后（用户在群里粘贴），纳入 Step 4 最终报告
- 如果到 Step 4 时外部结果仍未返回，调用 `get_external_review_status(project)` 确认状态，在报告中标注

### Step 0.7 — 视觉审查派发（与 Step 1 并行）

派发独立视觉审查 Agent，与 Reviewer 审稿并行执行：

```
dispatch_visual_check(project="{project}", review_chat_id="{review_chat_id}")
```

- 视觉审查 Agent 自动渲染论文 PDF 并逐页检查排版质量（Figure 1 位置、布局节奏、图表质量、空白分布等）
- **不参与评分和交叉讨论**，结果仅作为参考信息
- 启动和完成通知自动发送到 Group C
- 结果在 Step 4 通过 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读取并拼入报告
- **fire-and-forget**：调用立即返回，本步骤永不等待视觉审查完成

### Step 1 — Round N：独立审稿

携带 Step 0 搜到的 venue 要求，启动所有 Reviewer：

```
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="1", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
...（按需）
```

消息中必须包含：
- venue 名称和截止日期
- 页数限制和模板名称
- 匿名规则
- 论文文件路径
- **该 Reviewer 的审查侧重**（在消息中明确指定）

收集所有 Reviewer 的审稿结果。

### Step 2 — 交叉分享（原文转发 + 逐条回应）

将每位 Reviewer 的**完整审稿原文**转发给其他 Reviewer，要求逐条回应：

```
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="""
以下是 Reviewer 1 的完整审稿意见：

{Reviewer 1 的原文}

请逐条回应：[AGREE] 同意并说明理由，或 [REBUT] 反驳并提供证据（cite 具体 Section/Table/Figure）。
""")
```

对每位 Reviewer 重复此步骤（每人看到其他所有 Reviewer 的原文）。

收集所有交叉回应。

### Step 3 — 收敛判断

分析所有 Reviewer 的意见和交叉回应：

- **关键问题已达成共识**（`[AGREE]` 占多数，无未解决的 `[REBUT]` 矛盾）→ 进入 Step 4
- **存在重大分歧**（关键 issue 上有 `[REBUT]` 且双方各有道理）→ 回到 Step 1 开始下一轮，附带聚焦问题
- **最多 3 轮**：如果第 3 轮仍有分歧，在报告中如实记录各方观点

### Step 4 — 汇总报告 & 投递

合并所有轮次的发现，形成统一审稿报告：

1. 报告结构：
   - **Summary**：论文概述（2-3 句）
   - **Strengths**：优点（逐条列出）
   - **Weaknesses**：缺点（逐条列出，这是重点，必须严格）
   - **Reviewer Consensus**：所有 Reviewer 达成共识的关键问题（标注 `[AGREE]`）
   - **Reviewer Divergence**：分歧点及各方理由（标注 `[REBUT]`，如有）
   - **Questions**：需要作者澄清的问题
   - **Missing References**：遗漏的重要相关工作
   - **External Review (Stanford Agentic Reviewer)**：如有外部审稿结果，单独列出其 7 维评分、关键发现、以及与内部审稿的差异；如未返回则标注状态
   - **Visual Layout Check**（非评分项，不阻塞报告）：调用 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读一次状态——
     - `done` → 直接拼入 findings
     - `running` → 写"仍在进行中，本报告不等待，完成后会自动补发到 Group C"
     - `timeout` / `error` → 写失败原因 + 提示用户可重新触发
     - `not_started` → 写未派发
     不要为视觉审查推迟报告投递。视觉 Agent 完成后会自己把结果发到 Group C，与本报告解耦。可直接调用 `format_visual_findings_for_report(project)` 拿到现成的 markdown section
   - **Overall Assessment**：总评 + 评分（strong reject / weak reject / borderline / weak accept / strong accept）+ 置信度
   - **Detailed Comments**：逐节详细意见
2. **同步 Issue Tracker**（投递前必做）：
   - 用 `read_local_file("projects/{project}/artifacts/review_issues.yaml")` 读当前 tracker（不存在视为空）
   - 对本轮所有 Weakness/Must-Fix/Should-Fix:

## EMNLP 2026 Call for Papers - Submission Guidelines

### Overview
EMNLP 2026 invites the submission of long and short papers featuring substantial, original, and unpublished research on empirical methods for Natural Language Processing. EMNLP 2026 has a goal of curating a diverse technical program—in addition to traditional research results, papers may contribute negative findings, survey an area, announce the creation of a new resource, argue a position, report novel linguistic insights derived using existing computational techniques, and reproduce (or fail to reproduce) previous results.

### Important Dates
ARR submission deadline (long & short papers): May 25, 2026; Reviewer registration deadline for ALL authors: May 27, 2026; Author response and author-reviewer discussion: July 7 - July 13, 2026; Meta review released: July 30, 2026; EMNLP commitment deadline: August 2, 2026; Notification of acceptance (long & short papers): August 20, 2026; Camera-ready papers due (long & short): September 20, 2026; Main Conference (dates for Workshops/Tutorials TBD): October 22 - 26, 2026.

### Submission Process via ARR
Given that the ARR 2026 May cycle is aligned with two conferences (EMNLP and AACL), authors will need to explicitly declare which conference they intend to commit to at submission time. This choice will be binding for EMNLP 2026: i.e., ARR 2026 May submissions that do not select EMNLP 2026 during submission will not be able to commit to EMNLP 2026.

### Key Policies
- Dual submissions are not allowed!
- Following the ACL and ARR policies, there is no anonymity period requirement.
- The reviewing process will continue to be double-blind. Reviewers will not see authors, nor will authors see reviewers and reviews on ARR will not be made publicly visible.

For the complete details, visit the official EMNLP 2026 call for papers at https://2026.emnlp.org/calls/main_conference_papers/

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Execution traces record a program's complete runtime behavior: every function call, variable assignment, and control flow decision.
4	Recent work has incorporated them into code language models for tasks from bug localization to program repair \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}, under the working assumption that richer runtime information yields better predictions.
5	\emph{We find the opposite.}
6	For verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), feeding a model the complete execution trace produces accuracies of 79--82\%, barely above a source-code-only baseline (72--76\%), while a single compact component of the same trace reaches ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models tested.
7	Verbose traces do not just fail to help; they actively impair learning.
8	
9	Verdict prediction offers a clean testbed for isolating this effect.
10	As binary classification, it separates signal extraction from generation noise; as fault detection, the model need only detect failure, not simulate execution.
11	If the fault signal concentrates in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
12	Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation tasks where this density hypothesis could not be cleanly tested.
13	
14	We conduct the first systematic component ablation of trace representations, decomposing VOTA (exception events + assertion comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families \citep{qwen2025coder,roziere2024code,deepseek2024coder}, on 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}.
15	The results are unambiguous: exception events (a median of 150 tokens encoding error type, stack frame, and message) reach ${\geq}$99.33\% accuracy across all models and seeds, converging within 50 training steps.
16	Full traces plateau near 82\% and gradient-masked variants reach only ${\sim}$86\%, both without stable convergence. This confirms that information density, not model capacity, is the binding constraint (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).
17	
18	This finding is robust to several potential confounds.
19	Removing format markers preserves accuracy within 2pp, and on 8 boundary samples where exceptions appear in passing code, the fine-tuned model correctly classifies 6/8 vs.\ 0/8 for a regex baseline, which confirms the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
20	Gradient masking bounds the backward-pass contribution to ${\sim}$4pp (\S\ref{sec:density}), a tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}), and cross-dataset transfer to DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the component ranking (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
21	
22	Our contributions:
23	\begin{enumerate}
24	\item \textbf{Information density as the binding constraint on SFT learning}: training dynamics, gradient masking (${\sim}$4pp backward-pass contribution), and cross-model convergence confirm that compact trace inputs learn faster and more stably than verbose ones, independent of model scale (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:density}).
25	\item \textbf{Exception events as the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models with zero cross-seed variance on Qwen and sub-1pp cross-model range (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
26	\item \textbf{A two-tier diagnostic hierarchy with quantitative decomposition}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertion comparisons) are individually sufficient for near-perfect accuracy and generalize across architectures within a 0.50--1.11pp cross-model range, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) are model-dependent with ${\sim}$9pp range; a sharp phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens spatially localizes the diagnostic boundary (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
27	\end{enumerate}
28	
29	\begin{figure}[t]
30	\centering
31	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
32	\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy by trace condition (Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B vs.\ DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, $N{=}1{,}190$). \cond{exception\_only} shows near-identical accuracy across models ($\Delta{=}0.5$pp), while \cond{VOTA} exhibits a 15pp cross-model gap due to a tokenizer-induced training failure (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).}
33	\label{fig:cross_scale}
34	\end{figure}

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces record a program's complete runtime behavior: every function call, variable assignment, and control flow decision.
Recent work has incorporated them into code language models for tasks from bug localization to program repair \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}, under the working assumption that richer runtime information yields better predictions.
\emph{We find the opposite.}
For verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), feeding a model the complete execution trace produces accuracies of 79--82\%, barely above a source-code-only baseline (72--76\%), while a single compact component of the same trace reaches ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models tested.
Verbose traces do not just fail to help; they actively impair learning.

Verdict prediction offers a clean testbed for isolating this effect.
As binary classification, it separates signal extraction from generation noise; as fault detection, the model need only detect failure, not simulate execution.
If the fault signal concentrates in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation tasks where this density hypothesis could not be cleanly tested.

We conduct the first systematic component ablation of trace representations, decomposing VOTA (exception events + assertion comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families \citep{qwen2025coder,roziere2024code,deepseek2024coder}, on 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}.
The results are unambiguous: exception events (a median of 150 tokens encoding error type, stack frame, and message) reach ${\geq}$99.33\% accuracy across all models and seeds, converging within 50 training steps.
Full traces plateau near 82\% and gradient-masked variants reach only ${\sim}$86\%, both without stable convergence. This confirms that information density, not model capacity, is the binding constraint (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).

This finding is robust to several potential confounds.
Removing format markers preserves accuracy within 2pp, and on 8 boundary samples where exceptions appear in passing code, the fine-tuned model correctly classifies 6/8 vs.\ 0/8 for a regex baseline, which confirms the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
Gradient masking bounds the backward-pass contribution to ${\sim}$4pp (\S\ref{sec:density}), a tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}), and cross-dataset transfer to DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the component ranking (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Information density as the binding constraint on SFT learning}: training dynamics, gradient masking (${\sim}$4pp backward-pass contribution), and cross-model convergence confirm that compact trace inputs learn faster and more stably than verbose ones, independent of model scale (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Exception events as the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models with zero cross-seed variance on Qwen and sub-1pp cross-model range (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
\item \textbf{A two-tier diagnostic hierarchy with quantitative decomposition}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertion comparisons) are individually sufficient for near-perfect accuracy and generalize across architectures within a 0.50--1.11pp cross-model range, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) are model-dependent with ${\sim}$9pp range; a sharp phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens spatially localizes the diagnostic boundary (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy by trace condition (Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B vs.\ DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, $N{=}1{,}190$). \cond{exception\_only} shows near-identical accuracy across models ($\Delta{=}0.5$pp), while \cond{VOTA} exhibits a 15pp cross-model gap due to a tokenizer-induced training failure (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).}
\label{fig:cross_scale}
\end{figure}

2	
3	We presented the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction, covering four code models across three architecture families.
4	The finding is clear: information density, not trace completeness, determines learning efficiency under SFT.
5	Compact exception events converge to ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models, while verbose full traces oscillate without stable convergence.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction, covering four code models across three architecture families.
The finding is clear: information density, not trace completeness, determines learning efficiency under SFT.
Compact exception events converge to ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models, while verbose full traces oscillate without stable convergence.
These results establish a two-tier diagnostic hierarchy: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertion comparisons) generalize across architectures within a 0.50--1.11pp range, while Tier~2 signals (loop patterns) are model-dependent. For structurally constrained tasks such as verdict prediction, targeted signal extraction should replace wholesale trace inclusion.

103	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
104	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
105	
106	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
107	
108	\begin{algorithm}[h!]
109	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
110	\label{alg:vota}
111	\small
112	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
113	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
114	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
115	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
116	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
117	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
118	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
119	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
120	\ENDFOR
121	\IF{no exception events found}
122	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
123	\ENDIF
124	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
125	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
126	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
127	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
128	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
129	\ENDFOR
130	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
131	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
132	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
133	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
134	  \ENDIF
135	\ENDFOR
136	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
137	\RETURN $V$
138	\end{algorithmic}
139	\end{algorithm}

142	\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
143	\label{sec:vota_examples}
144	
145	We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
146	In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
147	In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.
148	
149	\paragraph{Fail example.}
150	A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.
151	
152	\begin{scriptsize}
153	\begin{verbatim}
154	## Function
155	def divide(a, b):
156	    return a / b
157	
158	## Test Input
159	divide(1, 0)
160	
161	## Expected Output
162	inf
163	
164	## VOTA Trace
165	[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
166	
167	## Verdict
168	fail
169	\end{verbatim}
170	\end{scriptsize}
171	
172	\paragraph{Pass example.}
173	No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.
174	
175	\begin{scriptsize}
176	\begin{verbatim}
177	## Function
178	def add(a, b):
179	    return a + b
180	
181	## Test Input
182	add(2, 3)
183	
184	## Expected Output
185	5
186	
187	## VOTA Trace
188	[LOOP] No loops detected.
189	[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5
190	
191	## Verdict
192	pass
193	\end{verbatim}
194	\end{scriptsize}
195	
196	These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.

284	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
285	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
286	
287	DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
288	Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, which confirms complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
289	The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
290	Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
291	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
292	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
293	Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).
294	
295	A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
296	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.
297	
298	Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
299	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).
300

302	\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
303	\label{sec:irreducible}
304	
305	The \textit{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
306	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
307	
308	\begin{itemize}
309	\item \textbf{Function:} \textit{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
310	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \textit{pass}.
311	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \textit{fail} (false negative).
312	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, which indicates a systematic rather than stochastic error.
313	\end{itemize}
314	
315	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \textit{check\_dict\_case} uses \textit{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \textit{all()} short-circuits on the first \textit{True} value, raising \textit{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
316	Because \textit{GeneratorExit} is a \textit{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \textit{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
317	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \textit{fail}.
318	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \textit{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \textit{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
319	
320	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
321	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
322	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
323	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

425	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
426	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
427	The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
428	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
429	Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.
430	
431	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
432	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), which confirms that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
433	The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
434	The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).
435	
436	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
437	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
438	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
439	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
440	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
441	
442	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
443	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
444	Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.
445	
446	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%). This indicates that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
447	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
448	This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.
449	
450	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
451	The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

597	\section{Error Overlap Analysis}
598	\label{sec:error_overlap}
599	
600	We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).
601	
602	\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors (samples 901 and 905) have zero intersection with the error sets of all other conditions (Jaccard = 0.000 in all pairwise comparisons).
603	This orthogonality arises because \texttt{exception\_only} errors are caused by \texttt{GeneratorExit} false positives (pass samples misclassified as fail due to benign \texttt{BaseException} events), while errors from other conditions are predominantly fail samples misclassified as pass due to insufficient signal.
604	
605	Among non-exception conditions, error sets exhibit hierarchical containment: \texttt{ae\_only} $\subset$ VOTA $\subset$ \texttt{loop\_only} $\subset$ \texttt{no\_trace}, with pairwise Jaccard indices increasing with signal overlap.
606	\texttt{loop\_only} and \texttt{full\_trace} share the highest overlap (Jaccard ${\sim}$0.65), reflecting their shared reliance on behavioral patterns rather than explicit fault indicators.
607	
608	This analysis confirms that \texttt{exception\_only} operates on an independent signal dimension: its errors are representation ambiguities (iterator protocol artifacts) rather than information deficits, explaining why combining it with other signals cannot eliminate these specific errors.

613	\section{Cross-Dataset Generalization: DebugBench}
614	\label{sec:debugbench_full}
615	
616	To test whether exception-based verdict prediction generalizes beyond LLM-generated solutions, we evaluate on DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench}, a dataset of human-written programs with synthetically injected bugs (single-point mutations such as operator replacement, variable misuse, and missing statements).
617	After filtering for executable Python samples with valid traces, we retain 426 samples with a near-balanced class distribution (majority baseline: 51.4\%).

637	Table~\ref{tab:debugbench} shows that the component ranking from the main experiments is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} (100.00\%) $\geq$ VOTA (99.77\%) $>$ \texttt{no\_trace} (96.71\%).
638	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition achieves perfect accuracy. This confirms that the exception-based representation generalizes to a different fault distribution without degradation.
639	
640	The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
641	This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
642	In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.
643	
644	These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
645	The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.

648	\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
649	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
650	
651	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
652	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
653	All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
654	VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
655	This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
656	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
657	The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
658	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.
659

661	\section{Training Dynamics}
662	\label{sec:training_dynamics}
663	
664	% fig:training_dynamics moved to main text (discussion.tex)
665	
666	The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
667	Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
668	Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
669	The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.
670	
671	The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
672	Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%. This confirms that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

681	The high duplication in \texttt{exception\_only} does not affect our experimental conclusions: after deduplication the training set still contains 2,858 unique samples and the test set 607, providing sufficient coverage for the 591-problem benchmark.
682	
683	\paragraph{Problem-level partitioning and sensitivity analysis.}
684	Data is partitioned at the problem level: 472 training problems and 119 test problems, with zero crossover.
685	Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
686	To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a 0.00pp accuracy delta in every case.
687	This confirms that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[h!]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
\label{sec:vota_examples}

We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.

\paragraph{Fail example.}
A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

## Test Input
divide(1, 0)

## Expected Output
inf

## VOTA Trace
[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

## Verdict
fail
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

\paragraph{Pass example.}
No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

## Test Input
add(2, 3)

## Expected Output
5

## VOTA Trace
[LOOP] No loops detected.
[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5

## Verdict
pass
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, which confirms complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \textit{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \textit{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \textit{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \textit{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, which indicates a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \textit{check\_dict\_case} uses \textit{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \textit{all()} short-circuits on the first \textit{True} value, raising \textit{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \textit{GeneratorExit} is a \textit{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \textit{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \textit{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \textit{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \textit{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), which confirms that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%). This indicates that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{tail-256} & \textbf{tail-384} & \textbf{tail-512} & \textbf{tail-1024} & \textbf{tail-2048} & \textbf{exc\_only} \\
\midrule
Qwen-7B (7B) & 78.9 & 79.9 & 93.6 & 96.5 & 97.3 & 99.83 \\
DeepSeek (6.7B) & 76.4 & 82.9 & 93.9 & 96.5 & 95.0$\downarrow$ & 99.33 \\
CodeLlama (13B) & 77.9 & 80.6 & 98.2 & 98.2$^\dag$ & 41.8$^\ddag$ & 99.89 \\
Qwen-1.5B (1.5B) & 72.6 & 73.6 & 95.6 & 96.6 & 97.9 & 99.83 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Cross-model truncation direction comparison ($N{=}1{,}190$). Head-truncation retains the first 2,048 tokens; tail-truncation retains the last 2,048. All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 signal-poor band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp). $^\dag$CodeLlama tail-2048 pending retraining (\S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).}
\label{tab:head_vs_tail}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{head-2048 (\%)} & \textbf{tail-2048 (\%)} & \textbf{Gap (pp)} \\
\midrule
Qwen-1.5B & 75.3 & 97.9 & +22.6 \\
DeepSeek-6.7B & 78.7 & 95.0 & +16.3 \\
CodeLlama-13B & 79.9 & ---$^\dag$ & ---$^\dag$ \\
Qwen-7B & 81.8 & 97.3 & +15.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Four patterns emerge from the budget curve.
\emph{Phase transition between 384 and 512 tokens}: the tail-384 column reveals that the transition is not instantaneous at 256$\to$512 but localized between 384 and 512 tokens.
At tail-384, all four models remain near baseline (73.6--82.9\%), gaining only +1.0--6.5pp over tail-256.
The steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512: +13.7pp (Qwen-7B), +11.0pp (DeepSeek), +17.6pp (CodeLlama), +22.0pp (Qwen-1.5B), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling.
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, consistent with the typical exception traceback length: below ${\sim}$384 tokens, the traceback is truncated and no diagnostic event is captured; above ${\sim}$512, it is fully included regardless of model capacity or architecture.

\emph{Convergence at tail-512+}: once the phase transition is crossed, accuracy converges across all models into a 93.6--98.2\% band at tail-512 (seed 42).
Multi-seed validation confirms robustness: across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations at tail-512 (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}), all accuracies fall within [93.61\%, 98.24\%], a 4.63pp band that compresses the signal-poor tail-256 spread (6.3pp) by 27\%.
CodeLlama-13B shows perfect per-model convergence at tail-512: all three seeds achieve 98.24\% ($\sigma{=}$0), consistent with the 13B scale and label-only loss providing a stronger optimization signal in the signal-rich regime (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}).

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Cross-seed convergence at the tail-512 truncation point ($N{=}1{,}190$ per seed). All 12 model$\times$seed combinations fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%]. CodeLlama-13B achieves identical accuracy across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}$0).}
\label{tab:tail512_seeds}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccccr}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{S42} & \textbf{S123} & \textbf{S456} & \textbf{Mean} & \textbf{$\sigma$} \\
\midrule
Qwen-7B (7B)      & 93.61 & 96.00 & 97.65 & 95.75 & 2.05 \\
DeepSeek (6.7B)    & 93.95 & 95.04 & 96.10 & 95.03 & 1.08 \\
Qwen-1.5B (1.5B)  & 95.63 & 97.65 & 96.72 & 96.67 & 1.01 \\
CodeLlama (13B)    & 98.24 & 98.24 & 98.24 & \textbf{98.24} & \textbf{0.00} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{Cross-model band} & \multicolumn{2}{r}{[93.61, 98.24] = 4.63pp} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

At tail-1024, four models reach 96.5--98.2\% (CodeLlama 98.2\% under label-only loss, three others 96.5--96.6\%).
Scale and architecture differences that dominate the signal-poor regime (tail-256 range: 72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp) compress dramatically in the signal-rich regime.

\emph{Signal-poor convergence band}: head-2048 accuracies across all four models also converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp; Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}), comparable in width to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp).
When the diagnostic signal is absent (head-truncation discards trace terminus) or unreachable (tail-256 is too short), models of different scale and architecture collapse to similar performance, suggesting a shared floor determined by code comprehension rather than trace processing.

\emph{Scale behavior inversion}: in the signal-poor regime (tail-256), smaller models perform worse (Qwen-1.5B 72.6\% vs.\ Qwen-7B 78.9\%, $-$6.3pp), mirroring the \texttt{no\_trace} scale pattern.
In the signal-rich regime (tail-512+), this reverses: Qwen-1.5B matches or exceeds Qwen-7B (95.6\% vs.\ 93.6\% at tail-512; 97.9\% vs.\ 97.3\% at tail-2048), which confirms that sufficient trace signal eliminates the capacity advantage.

\emph{Non-monotonicity at long sequences}: two models show accuracy decreases beyond tail-1024.
DeepSeek-6.7B drops $-$1.5pp from tail-1024 (96.5\%) to tail-2048 (95.0\%), consistent with its known long-context sensitivity (\S\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
CodeLlama-13B exhibits a more severe collapse: tail-2048 under label-only loss drops to 41.8\% (vs.\ tail-1024 = 98.2\%), which we attribute to LoRA long-sequence instability under the label-only loss regime; this outlier is excluded from cross-model tail-2048 analysis.
Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B increase monotonically across all budgets.

Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail} confirms the truncation direction effect: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 outperforms head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp.
The gap is largest for Qwen-1.5B (+22.6pp). This indicates that smaller models benefit most from positional proximity to the diagnostic signal, as they lack the capacity to locate it within longer, noisier prefixes.

%% ============================================================
\section{Calibration Analysis}
\label{sec:calibration_full}

Beyond accuracy, we evaluate whether trace conditions affect prediction calibration, motivated by recent findings that code LLM confidence is often poorly calibrated \citep{spiess2025calibration}.

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Calibration metrics on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). ECE = expected calibration error; Brier = Brier score. Lower is better for both.}
\label{tab:calibration}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{ECE $\downarrow$} & \textbf{Brier $\downarrow$} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & \textbf{0.0004} & \textbf{0.0008} \\
exception\_only & 0.0027 & 0.0013 \\
VOTA & 0.0054 & 0.005 \\
full\_trace & 0.096 & 0.144 \\
no\_trace & 0.171 & 0.197 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:calibration} shows that calibration quality mirrors the Tier~1/2 hierarchy.
Tier~1 conditions (\texttt{ae\_only}: ECE=0.0004; \texttt{exception\_only}: ECE=0.0027) produce near-perfectly calibrated predictions, while \texttt{full\_trace} (ECE=0.096) and \texttt{no\_trace} (ECE=0.171) exhibit substantial miscalibration.
VOTA (ECE=0.0054) is well-calibrated but slightly worse than either Tier~1 component alone, reinforcing the pattern that combining trace signals dilutes rather than improves the prediction signal.

The Brier scores tell a consistent story: \texttt{ae\_only} (0.0008) and \texttt{exception\_only} (0.0013) achieve near-zero scores, while \texttt{no\_trace} (0.197) indicates substantial miscalibration.

\paragraph{Cross-model calibration.}
Table~\ref{tab:calibration_cross} extends the calibration analysis to four models (1.5B--13B) under \texttt{exception\_only}.
All four models achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007 and Brier ${<}$ 0.007, which confirms that calibration quality generalizes across architectures and scales.
CodeLlama-13B achieves the lowest ECE (0.0020) and MCE (0.0411), while DeepSeek-6.7B shows the highest ECE (0.0064) and Brier (0.0061), consistent with its higher error rate (8 errors vs.\ 2 for Qwen/CodeLlama).

\centering
\caption{Cross-model calibration for \texttt{exception\_only} ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). ECE = expected calibration error; Brier = Brier score; MCE = maximum calibration error. All four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007.}
\label{tab:calibration_cross}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{ECE $\downarrow$} & \textbf{Brier $\downarrow$} & \textbf{MCE $\downarrow$} \\
\midrule
Qwen-1.5B & \textbf{0.0020} & \textbf{0.0013} & --- \\
CodeLlama-13B & \textbf{0.0020} & \textbf{0.0013} & \textbf{0.0411} \\
Qwen-7B & 0.0027 & \textbf{0.0013} & 0.8355 \\

%% ============================================================
\section{Error Overlap Analysis}
\label{sec:error_overlap}

We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).

\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors (samples 901 and 905) have zero intersection with the error sets of all other conditions (Jaccard = 0.000 in all pairwise comparisons).
This orthogonality arises because \texttt{exception\_only} errors are caused by \texttt{GeneratorExit} false positives (pass samples misclassified as fail due to benign \texttt{BaseException} events), while errors from other conditions are predominantly fail samples misclassified as pass due to insufficient signal.

Among non-exception conditions, error sets exhibit hierarchical containment: \texttt{ae\_only} $\subset$ VOTA $\subset$ \texttt{loop\_only} $\subset$ \texttt{no\_trace}, with pairwise Jaccard indices increasing with signal overlap.
\texttt{loop\_only} and \texttt{full\_trace} share the highest overlap (Jaccard ${\sim}$0.65), reflecting their shared reliance on behavioral patterns rather than explicit fault indicators.

This analysis confirms that \texttt{exception\_only} operates on an independent signal dimension: its errors are representation ambiguities (iterator protocol artifacts) rather than information deficits, explaining why combining it with other signals cannot eliminate these specific errors.

% fig:error_overlap moved to main text (experiments.tex)

%% ============================================================
\section{Cross-Dataset Generalization: DebugBench}
\label{sec:debugbench_full}

To test whether exception-based verdict prediction generalizes beyond LLM-generated solutions, we evaluate on DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench}, a dataset of human-written programs with synthetically injected bugs (single-point mutations such as operator replacement, variable misuse, and missing statements).
After filtering for executable Python samples with valid traces, we retain 426 samples with a near-balanced class distribution (majority baseline: 51.4\%).

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Generalization to DebugBench ($N{=}426$, Qwen-2.5-7B, seed=42). Wilson 95\% CIs. The component ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is preserved, and exception\_only achieves perfect accuracy.}
\label{tab:debugbench}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{100.00} & [99.14, 100.00] \\
VOTA & 99.77 & [99.30, 100.00] \\
no\_trace & 96.71 & [94.80, 98.40] \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & 51.41 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:debugbench} shows that the component ranking from the main experiments is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} (100.00\%) $\geq$ VOTA (99.77\%) $>$ \texttt{no\_trace} (96.71\%).
The \texttt{exception\_only} condition achieves perfect accuracy. This confirms that the exception-based representation generalizes to a different fault distribution without degradation.

The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.

These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.

%% ============================================================
\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

%% ============================================================
\section{Training Dynamics}
\label{sec:training_dynamics}

% fig:training_dynamics moved to main text (discussion.tex)

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%. This confirms that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

%% ============================================================
\section{Deduplication Statistics}
\label{sec:dedup_stats}

Table~\ref{tab:dedup} reports the duplication rates across trace formats.
Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format (correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic), the dataset contains duplicate rows.
Train--test input overlap is zero (split by problem ID), so no information leakage occurs.
The high duplication in \texttt{exception\_only} does not affect our experimental conclusions: after deduplication the training set still contains 2,858 unique samples and the test set 607, providing sufficient coverage for the 591-problem benchmark.

\paragraph{Problem-level partitioning and sensitivity analysis.}
Data is partitioned at the problem level: 472 training problems and 119 test problems, with zero crossover.
Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a 0.00pp accuracy delta in every case.
This confirms that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.
The \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs due to representation compactness; all confidence intervals treat samples as independent Bernoulli trials.

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Deduplication statistics. The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses multiple passing solutions into identical rows because correct executions produce no exception events. Train--test input overlap is 0 (no leakage).}
\label{tab:dedup}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Split} & \textbf{Total} & \textbf{Unique} & \textbf{Dup.\ rate} \\
\midrule
exception\_only train & 4{,}720 & 2{,}858 & 39.45\% \\
exception\_only test  & 1{,}190 &   607 & 48.99\% \\
raw\_traces (full)    & 5{,}910 & 5{,}803 &  1.81\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%% ============================================================
\section{Regex Baseline Analysis}
\label{sec:regex_baselines}

To establish a non-learning upper bound, we evaluate six regex-based baselines on the \texttt{exception\_only} test set ($N{=}1{,}190$) and two format-specific baselines on VOTA and \texttt{full\_trace} inputs.

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{Regex baseline accuracy ($N{=}1{,}190$). B4 is the strongest semantic baseline (6.22pp below SFT \texttt{exception\_only}, McNemar $p{<}.001$). B6 uses an error count threshold. $^\ddag$B5 exploits a data formatting artifact: the \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker is deterministically present in all pass samples, making this a format-level shortcut rather than a genuine exception-based heuristic.}
\label{tab:regex}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llc}
\toprule
\textbf{Baseline} & \textbf{Method} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} \\
\midrule
B1: \texttt{[ERROR]} presence & string match & 93.45 \\
B2: Traceback presence & string match & 71.51 \\
B3: Any keyword & union of B1+B2+Exception & 93.45 \\
B4: Exception type regex & regex on exception class names & \textbf{93.61} \\
B5: Format marker & \texttt{[No exception data]} $\to$ pass & 99.33$^\ddag$ \\
B6: Error count $\geq$2 & count threshold & 92.02 \\
\midrule
VOTA format regex & best regex on VOTA traces & 75.55 \\
full\_trace format regex & best regex on full traces & 77.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

The strongest legitimate baseline (B4, 93.61\%) applies regex pattern-matching on Python exception class names (e.g., \texttt{ValueError}, \texttt{TypeError}).
Its errors concentrate on 8 boundary samples where a \texttt{ValueError} is raised inside a \texttt{try/except} block and caught; the program passes despite an exception occurring in the trace.
SFT \texttt{exception\_only} correctly classifies 6 of these 8 samples. This indicates that the model learns the semantic distinction between caught (benign) and uncaught (fault-indicating) exceptions.
B5 (99.33\%) achieves near-SFT accuracy but relies on the deterministic presence of a format marker in pass-class traces, which is an artifact of the trace preprocessing pipeline rather than a generalizable signal; the McNemar test vs.\ SFT ($p{=}.041$) confirms a statistically significant difference.

\paragraph{Cross-format comparison.}
Table~\ref{tab:regex_cross_format} compares SFT and the best applicable regex baseline for each trace format.
The SFT advantage increases with format complexity: \texttt{no\_trace} (+3.62pp over majority baseline) $<$ \texttt{full\_trace} (+4.37pp) $<$ \texttt{exception\_only} (+6.22pp) $\ll$ VOTA (+23.86pp).
The VOTA gap is largest because its structured multi-component format carries semantic content that regex cannot parse, while \texttt{exception\_only}'s simpler format allows regex to capture most of the signal.

\begin{table}[h!]
\centering
\caption{SFT vs.\ best regex baseline by trace format ($N{=}1{,}190$). Regex baselines: majority class for \texttt{no\_trace}, keyword matching for \texttt{full\_trace}, pattern matching for VOTA, exception type regex (B4) for \texttt{exception\_only}.}
\label{tab:regex_cross_format}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Format} & \textbf{SFT (\%)} & \textbf{Regex (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ (pp)} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & 99.83 & 93.61 & +6.22 \\
VOTA & 99.05 & 75.55 & +23.50 \\
full\_trace & 81.76 & 77.39 & +4.37 \\
no\_trace & 75.13 & 71.51 & +3.62 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Cross-Model Zero-Shot Comparison}
\label{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}

Table~\ref{tab:zeroshot_cross_model} compares zero-shot and SFT \texttt{exception\_only} accuracy across four models.
Zero-shot performance does not correlate with model size: the smallest model (Qwen-1.5B, 93.45\%) outperforms all larger models, while the largest (CodeLlama-13B) falls below majority baseline.
SFT compresses the 42.44pp zero-shot range to 0.50pp, eliminating architecture-dependent variance.

\centering
\caption{Zero-shot vs.\ SFT \texttt{exception\_only} across four models ($N{=}1{,}190$). Zero-shot accuracy is uncorrelated with model size; SFT normalizes cross-architecture variance from 42.44pp to 0.50pp.}
\label{tab:zeroshot_cross_model}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Size} & \textbf{Zero-shot (\%)} & \textbf{SFT (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ (pp)} \\
\midrule
Qwen-1.5B & 1.5B & 93.45 & 99.83 & +6.38 \\
DeepSeek-6.7B & 6.7B & 90.59 & 99.39 & +8.80 \\
Qwen-7B & 7B & 89.08 & 99.83 & +10.75 \\
CodeLlama-13B & 13B & 51.01 & 99.89 & +48.88 \\
\midrule
Range & --- & 42.44pp & 0.50pp & --- \\

\end{tabular}%
}
